analysis.one_liner: Requires the FDA to revoke approval of one opioid painkiller every time it approves a new one.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote; it was referred to the Senate HELP Committee in March 2023 and died there when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have changed how the FDA handles opioid pain medications: every time the agency approves a new opioid drug, it would be required to strip approval from an existing one, prioritizing the removal of formulations that are not designed to deter abuse. Its stated aim was to shrink the number of prescription opioids on the market in response to the overdose epidemic. It was introduced by Senator Joe Manchin with one Republican cosponsor and never advanced past its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: People at risk of opioid addiction and overdose, and communities affected by the roughly 100,000-plus annual overdose deaths the bill's findings cite; the bill sought to reduce the supply of prescription opioids by forcing one existing drug off the market with each new approval.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FDA to revoke approval of one previously approved opioid pain medication for every new opioid it approves, steadily reducing the number of opioid drugs on the market.
Directs the FDA to prioritize revoking approval of opioid formulations that are not abuse-deterrent and to consider each drug's public health impact when choosing which drug to remove.
Cites the finding that two-thirds of the more than 107,000 U.S. overdose deaths in 2021 involved prescription or synthetic opioids, framing the bill as a response to the overdose death toll.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical companies that make opioid pain medications would lose an approved product each time a new opioid is approved. Some patients with severe or chronic pain could also lose access if the drug removed from the market was one that worked for them, since the removal is triggered by arithmetic rather than a finding about the specific drug's safety.
analysis.who_pays_short: Opioid painkiller makers, and some pain patients

drawbacks.text: The one-for-one rule is mechanical: a drug could be removed from the market not because it was found unsafe, but simply because a new opioid was approved, leaving patients who rely on it to find alternatives.

The bill overrides the FDA's normal judgment with a statutory mandate, even though the findings in the bill itself acknowledge that recent overdose deaths are driven substantially by illicit synthetic opioids rather than newly approved prescription products.
A narrower opioid supply could leave some patients with serious pain, such as cancer or post-surgical pain, with fewer treatment options.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The goal — fewer prescription opioids in circulation after an epidemic that has killed hundreds of thousands — is serious and widely shared. But the mechanism is blunt: tying revocations one-for-one to new approvals removes drugs by arithmetic rather than by evidence about which drugs are doing harm, and it does nothing about the illicit fentanyl supply driving most current deaths. A more targeted version would give the FDA discretion to act on the riskiest products; this bill trades precision for a hard cap.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Joe Manchin introduced the bill on March 1, 2023, with Senator Mike Braun as a cosponsor.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — appears in the bill's action history for the remainder of the 118th Congress, which ended January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers of opioid pain medications, who keep their full approved portfolios, since no drug was ever removed under the bill's rule. Patients who depend on a specific opioid also avoided the risk of losing access to it.

for.name: Sen. Mike Braun
for.role: U.S. Senator from Indiana; 1 of 49 Senate Republicans cosponsoring

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote appears in the record for the two years before the Congress ended.

against.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration during his chairmanship.

sides.party_line_note: There was no vote to measure partisanship; the bill's sponsorship was bipartisan, a Democrat from West Virginia with one Republican cosponsor, and it never reached a roll call.

industries.note: Each new opioid approval would have cost one existing product its FDA approval, shrinking the market for prescription opioids over time. Public health groups have long pointed to heavy marketing and overprescribing of these products as a driver of the addiction epidemic, so the industry's interest here ran against the bill's public-health aim.

Because the bill tells the FDA to prioritize removing opioids that are not abuse-deterrent, makers of harder-to-abuse formulations would be relatively protected while standard formulations face removal first. Whether abuse-deterrent designs actually reduce overdose deaths is debated, but the bill clearly tilts the market in their favor.
